questions.prompt: Match backend frameworks to their common strengths.
questions.explanation: Framework choice depends on language, team style, and structure needs. FastAPI gives typed validation and docs; Flask is minimal; NestJS is opinionated.

pairs.right: Typed Python APIs with validation and OpenAPI

answer.FastAPI: Typed Python APIs with validation and OpenAPI

concept_panel.title: Backend Framework Trade-offs
concept_panel.explanation: Backend frameworks provide routing, request parsing, response generation, and extension points. FastAPI emphasizes Python type hints, Pydantic validation, async support, and generated OpenAPI docs. Flask is smaller and more flexible, while Express is the lightweight Node.js equivalent and NestJS adds more structure for TypeScript teams. The best framework choice depends on team language, project size, validation needs, and operational conventions.
key_takeaways: Frameworks shape routing and request handling.
FastAPI is strong for typed Python APIs.
Express is lightweight; NestJS is more structured.
concept_panel.interview_insight: Interviewers usually ask this concept to evaluate whether you can choose backend tools based on constraints rather than popularity.
concept_panel.practical_example: Choose FastAPI when Python typing and automatic OpenAPI docs are useful; choose Express for a small Node API.

questions.prompt: A JavaScript team needs a lightweight REST API. Which framework is the natural fit?
questions.explanation: Express is a lightweight Node.js web framework commonly used for REST APIs.

questions.prompt: Order a typical FastAPI request lifecycle.
questions.explanation: Middleware wraps the request, routing selects the endpoint, dependency injection supplies objects such as DB sessions, and response models shape output.

concept_panel.title: Input Validation Boundary
concept_panel.explanation: Validation rejects malformed or unsafe input before business logic runs. That keeps core logic simpler and produces predictable errors for clients. In typed frameworks, schemas can validate shape, types, ranges, and required fields automatically. Validation is not just correctness; it is also a security and maintainability boundary.
key_takeaways: Validate before business logic.
Schemas make errors predictable.
Validation reduces security and data-quality risk.
concept_panel.interview_insight: Interviewers usually ask this concept to evaluate whether you understand backend boundaries and defensive API design.
concept_panel.practical_example: A request with age=-10 should fail validation before creating a user.

questions.prompt: Many endpoints need a database session, but tests should swap it out. What pattern helps?
questions.explanation: Dependency injection supplies shared objects without hardcoding construction, making endpoints easier to test and decouple.

concept_panel.title: Dependency Injection
concept_panel.explanation: Dependency injection supplies collaborators such as database sessions, settings, or services instead of constructing them inside the endpoint. This makes code easier to test because dependencies can be replaced. In FastAPI, `Depends` declares dependencies in endpoint signatures. The practical value is clear boundaries, not magic.
key_takeaways: Dependencies are supplied from the outside.
Tests can swap real dependencies for controlled ones.
Endpoints stay focused on request handling.
concept_panel.interview_insight: Interviewers usually ask this concept to evaluate whether you can design testable backend components.
concept_panel.practical_example: A test can override `get_db` with a temporary SQLite session.

questions.prompt: Which tasks belong in application lifespan startup?
questions.explanation: Lifespan startup runs once for shared initialization. Per-request validation belongs in request handling.

questions.explanation: Background tasks are useful when work can continue after the user receives the response.

concept_panel.title: Async, Concurrency, and Parallelism
concept_panel.explanation: Async helps a program make progress while waiting on I/O such as database calls or HTTP requests. It does not make CPU-heavy work faster by itself. Concurrency is about handling multiple tasks in overlapping time; parallelism is about running work at the same time on multiple CPU cores. Interviewers often test this because many candidates use `async` as a vague performance answer.
key_takeaways: Async helps I/O-bound work.
CPU-heavy work needs parallelism or workers.
Concurrency and parallelism are different concepts.
concept_panel.interview_insight: Interviewers usually ask this concept to evaluate whether you understand backend performance models.
concept_panel.practical_example: Awaiting a slow API call lets the server process other requests while it waits.

coding_challenges.title: Backend status classifier
coding_challenges.instructions: Implement classify_status_code(code: int) -> str. Return success for 200-299, redirect for 300-399, client_error for 400-499, server_error for 500-599, and unknown otherwise.
coding_challenges.explanation: The challenge reinforces deterministic branching, status-code categories, and local test execution.
